title: Job Search, Promotion, and Career Clarity: The Mid-Career GPS Podcast
author: John Neral
description: Get Clarity. Get Promoted. Get Hired. This show helps mid-career professionals navigate job searches, career advancement, and workplace challenges through actionable advice and expert interviews.

episodes.title: 366: Why Every Organization Needs a "Show Bible" with Robyn Hatcher
episodes.summary: Former soap opera writer Robyn Hatcher explains how understanding your organization's unwritten culture and communication patterns helps you handle conflict and advance, including her EDIT and LUVE frameworks for difficult conversations.

episodes.title: 365: Are You the Kind of Professional I Help?
episodes.summary: John explains why talented, dependable mid-career professionals can still feel invisible at work, what prompts people to seek career coaching, how coaching differs from therapy, and what coaching can realistically promise.

episodes.title: 364: Building Visibility When Work Is Shifting
episodes.summary: Back from a break, John talks about rebuilding confidence after disappointment, drawing on his experience on the PBA50 bowling tour and a three-question framework from Olympic champion Lanny Bassham for turning setbacks into better decisions.

episodes.title: 363: Have You Already Left Your Job in Your Head? How to Know When You've Crossed the Bridge
episodes.summary: John introduces the idea of crossing the bridge, the point where you've emotionally disengaged from a job before you've resigned, and offers a framework for recognizing it and deciding what to do next.

episodes.title: 362: How To Get Clear Feedback After A Missed Promotion
episodes.summary: Getting passed over hurts, and the silence afterward is worse. John explains exactly how to ask for feedback, how to listen to it, how to spot patterns, and how to tell whether your organization is developing your career or just managing your performance.

articles.question: How do you ask for feedback after being passed over for a promotion?
articles.metaDescription: Career coach John Neral gives the exact script for asking why you didn't get the promotion, how to listen without defending, and how to tell if your boss is developing you.
articles.intro: Ask directly, soon, and with a script: tell your leader you respect the decision and want to understand what skills to build to be considered next time, then listen without defending yourself. That's the approach career coach John Neral lays out on The Mid-Career GPS Podcast. He also explains how to read vague answers, how to tell whether your boss is developing your career or just managing your performance, and when the answer is to stop waiting and leave.

sections.heading: Ask for the conversation before the silence sets in
sections.body:
John's starting point is that the rejection itself isn't the worst part. The silence afterward is. When nobody explains why, you start writing the explanation yourself, and it's rarely a kind one.

So don't wait for your leader to bring it up. Most won't, because the conversation is uncomfortable for them too. Request it yourself, within days rather than weeks, and frame it so there's nothing for them to defend against. His suggested opener runs roughly like this: "I understand I wasn't selected for the position. I respect the decision. I'd like to understand what I can learn from this and what skills I should focus on to be considered for future opportunities. Can we have that conversation?"

Notice what that framing does. It closes the door on relitigating the decision and opens one on your future. That's a much easier yes for a manager.

quote.text: Being rejected is painful. But being rejected without an explanation is personal.
quote.speaker: John Neral

sections.heading: In the meeting: say thank you, then stop talking
sections.body:
Once you're in the room, John's rule is simple. Lead with gratitude, acknowledge that this is awkward for both of you, and then listen. Don't argue with the feedback, don't explain what really happened on that project, and don't try to re-interview for a job that's already been filled. The moment you get defensive, your leader stops being candid, and candor is the whole point.

Steer toward specifics. Ask which competencies or skills the selected person demonstrated that you didn't. Ask whether there's a blind spot you're not seeing. Ask what "ready" would look like from where they sit. Vague answers like "it just wasn't the right time" are a signal to gently ask again: "What would make it the right time?"

quote.text: Listen without defending. Don't argue, don't explain, don't try to re-interview for the job.
quote.speaker: John Neral

sections.heading: Is this a one-off or a pattern?
sections.body:
After the conversation, John wants you to zoom out. Is this the first time you've been passed over, or the third? A single miss can be timing, budget, or a stronger internal candidate. Repeated misses are data.

He suggests separating two possible explanations. One is a real readiness gap: a skill, a level of visibility, or an experience you genuinely lack, which you can go build. The other is politics or team dynamics: a leader who has a favorite, a reorg that keeps moving the target, or a culture where your role isn't valued. Feedback conversations help you tell the two apart. If you keep hearing specific, actionable gaps, work on them. If you keep hearing nothing, or the story changes every time, the problem probably isn't you.

sections.heading: Managing performance versus developing your career
sections.body:
This is the distinction John returns to most. Some leaders only ever talk to you about your current job: deliverables, deadlines, this quarter's numbers. Others also talk about where you're going: your goals, the roles you want, the exposure you need. The first kind is managing your performance. Only the second kind is developing your career.

His red flags are concrete. Your leader avoids the feedback conversation entirely. You ask more than once and still get nothing. Every one-on-one is about the present and never about the future. Growth conversations get brushed off as uncomfortable. If that's your situation, you can be an excellent performer and still be stuck, because nobody above you is invested in moving you.

quote.text: If your leader is only talking to you about your current job and is never talking to you about your future, your goals, your aspirations, they are only managing your performance, they are not developing your career.
quote.speaker: John Neral

sections.heading: Deciding whether to stay
sections.body:
John is direct about loyalty. Every two weeks, you've worked and they've paid you, and at that point you're even. Staying should be a decision you make because the organization invests in your growth, not a default you drift into.

He also warns about resentment. If you let a missed promotion fester, it shows: you disengage, your relationships sour, and your visibility drops, which makes the next promotion even less likely. So the choice is binary and intentional. Either use the feedback to close gaps and build relationships with the people who influence your next move inside the company, or take that same clarity and start looking outside. What you shouldn't do is let the silence become the story you tell about yourself.

quote.text: Not every organization deserves your loyalty if it refuses to invest in your growth.
quote.speaker: John Neral

keyTakeaways: Request the feedback conversation yourself within days, framed around what to build for next time, not why the decision was wrong.
In the meeting, lead with thanks, listen without defending, and push gently for specific competencies or blind spots.
Ask whether this is a first miss or a pattern, and whether the gap is a real readiness issue or politics.
A leader who only discusses your current job and never your future is managing performance, not developing your career.
Don't let resentment fester; either work the feedback inside the company or use it to look outside.

faq.q: How soon after being passed over should I ask for feedback?
faq.a: Quickly. John Neral says ambiguity creates anxiety, and waiting lets you fill in the blanks with your own story. Ask within days while the decision is fresh.

faq.q: What if my manager gives vague feedback like 'it wasn't the right time'?
faq.a: Follow up with specifics: what would 'the right time' look like, which skills did the selected person show, what would make you a clear choice next round. Repeated vagueness after several asks is itself a red flag.

faq.q: Should I quit after being passed over for a promotion?
faq.a: Not automatically. Use the feedback and the pattern to decide whether your organization is actually investing in your growth. If it is, close the gaps. If it repeatedly isn't, John says it may not deserve your loyalty.
